canonical_statement: The authors stated that all data generated or analyzed during the study are included in the article and that further inquiries can be directed to the corresponding author.
The review followed PRISMA reporting guidance and Cochrane Collaboration guidance.
Two researchers independently searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from database inception through November 7, 2024, without language or publication-date restrictions.
Bibliographies of previously published meta-analyses were manually reviewed for additional potentially eligible studies.
References were exported to Mendeley for duplicate removal, followed by title/abstract screening and full-text review; a third reviewer was used to resolve discrepancies.
Risk of bias in observational studies was assessed with ROBINS-I across seven domains, with overall judgments of low, moderate, serious, critical, or no information.
The meta-analysis used Review Manager version 5.4.1 and a random-effects model.
Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals were estimated for all outcomes, with P values below 0.05 treated as statistically significant.
Heterogeneity was assessed using I-squared and categorized as low below 25%, moderate from 25% to 70%, and high above 75%.
Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was used to investigate high heterogeneity by removing one study at a time.
Eligible designs included randomized controlled trials or observational studies, including cohort studies.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the pooled real-world evidence did not show significant differences between empagliflozin and dapagliflozin for myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, heart failure-related events, MACE, or all-cause death.
The authors stated that the analysis does not suggest a clear cardiovascular benefit of empagliflozin over dapagliflozin, or vice versa, as add-on therapy for type 2 diabetes.
The authors called for future head-to-head randomized controlled trials to determine whether one agent provides superior cardiovascular protection in specific patient subgroups.
The authors suggested that treatment selection should consider individual patient characteristics, side-effect profiles, treatment goals, cost, adherence, affordability, and accessibility.
The authors identified high heterogeneity as a major limitation, particularly for all-cause death and MACE.
The authors stated that heterogeneity may reflect differences in study design, patient populations, baseline characteristics, and cardiovascular outcome definitions.
The authors noted that real-world observational data are vulnerable to confounding, missing data, and treatment-adherence bias.
The authors stated that the absence of direct head-to-head randomized trials limits causal interpretation.
The MACE endpoint was defined differently across the pooled studies.

The source contains an internal sample-size inconsistency: 428,940 participants are reported in the Abstract, Results, and study table-derived totals, whereas the Discussion states 371,664 participants.

The PRISMA figure’s exclusion label conflicts with the text-defined eligibility and included-study descriptions because it lists observational studies among excluded reports while all eight included studies are described as observational.

The article discusses similar safety profiles and potential cost-effectiveness implications, but the meta-analysis outcomes extracted from the source do not include comparative safety or economic endpoints.
